#### You said:

- For **5D and 6D**, the result is airtight: the classification is complete.
- For **7D and above**, the classification of uniform polytopes is **not complete** (only the regular ones and prisms are fully enumerated). So strictly speaking, for n ≥ 7 it's a strong conjecture backed by the overdetermination argument, not a closed proof. But the degrees-of-freedom gap only grows with dimension, so no one expects a surprise.

**TL;DR:** Proven for 5D and 6D by exhaustive classification. For 7D+ it's a well-justified expectation from the counting argument, but not a closed theorem — the full classification simply hasn't been done. talking about snunbs. i need to know des it ever become uniform again

Worked for 59s

#### ChatGPT said:

If by **“snub” you mean the higher-dimensional analogue of the snub operation**, then **as far as currently known, it never becomes uniform again after 4D**.

The pattern is essentially:

DimensionUniform snub-type object?3D**Yes** — snub cube, snub dodecahedron, etc.4D**Yes** — the exceptional **snub 24-cell**5D**No known one**; e.g. the snub/full-snub 5-cube is nonuniform6D**No known one**; analogous snub constructions are nonuniform7D+**None known**

The 4D case is especially weird. The famous snub 24-cell is an exceptional uniform object tied to the D4/F4D_4/F_4 symmetry structure; its coordinates involve the golden ratio and its symmetry is unusually rich. [![](https://t0.gstatic.com/faviconV2?client=SOCIAL&type=FAVICON&fallback_opts=TYPE,SIZE,URL&url=https%3A%2F%2Farxiv.org&size=32&drop_404_icon=true)arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.3433?utm_source=chatgpt.com) In fact, terminology gets tricky: the commonly called **snub 24-cell is a “semi-snub”**; the *full* snub of the 24-cell is itself **not uniform**. [![](https://t0.gstatic.com/faviconV2?client=SOCIAL&type=FAVICON&fallback_opts=TYPE,SIZE,URL&url=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org&size=32&drop_404_icon=true)Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snub_24-cell?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Then the failure is already visible very concretely in 5D. The full snub 5-cube can be constructed, but the gaps require **irregular 5-cells**, so it is explicitly nonuniform. [![](https://t0.gstatic.com/faviconV2?client=SOCIAL&type=FAVICON&fallback_opts=TYPE,SIZE,URL&url=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org&size=32&drop_404_icon=true)Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stericated_5-cubes?utm_source=chatgpt.com) Similarly, a snub 6-demicube construction exists but contains irregular 5-simplexes, so it too is nonuniform. [![](https://t0.gstatic.com/faviconV2?client=SOCIAL&type=FAVICON&fallback_opts=TYPE,SIZE,URL&url=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org&size=32&drop_404_icon=true)Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stericated_6-orthoplexes?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

And here's an important correction to the text you quoted: **the complete classification of convex uniform polytopes is not known in 5D and 6D either.** A modern mathematical treatment states that the classification is complete only through dimension 4, and that it remains open whether non-prismatic, non-Wythoffian uniform polytopes exist in dimension 5+5+. [![](https://t0.gstatic.com/faviconV2?client=SOCIAL&type=FAVICON&fallback_opts=TYPE,SIZE,URL&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmartinwintermath.github.io&size=32&drop_404_icon=true)martinwintermath.github.io](https://martinwintermath.github.io/pdf/phd/thesis.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) So we cannot presently turn “none above 4D” into an absolute theorem covering every conceivable snub-like construction.

But the interesting part of your question is **could uniformity disappear at 5D/6D and then magically come back at, say, 8D or 11D?**

Mathematically, **nothing known suggests that it does**. The mechanism actually goes the wrong direction. A snub has only a small number of positional/truncation parameters, while uniformity demands that increasingly many independent classes of edges/facets simultaneously become regular. Higher dimension adds constraints much faster than it adds adjustable parameters. This is precisely why higher-dimensional alternations generally fail to be uniform: there are typically not enough degrees of freedom to rescale all the new pieces correctly. [![](https://t0.gstatic.com/faviconV2?client=SOCIAL&type=FAVICON&fallback_opts=TYPE,SIZE,URL&url=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org&size=32&drop_404_icon=true)Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternation_%28geometry%29?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

So I'd describe the sequence as:

3D: works → 4D: one spectacular exception → 5D+: no known comeback\boxed{\text{3D: works}\;\rightarrow\;\text{4D: one spectacular exception}\;\rightarrow\;\text{5D+: no known comeback}}

There's an even deeper reason **4D is suspiciously special**: the regular 24-cell and its F4/D4F_4/D_4 symmetry have **no analogue in dimensions above 4**. Coxeter explicitly describes the 24-cell as standing alone, with no higher-dimensional continuation. [![](https://t0.gstatic.com/faviconV2?client=SOCIAL&type=FAVICON&fallback_opts=TYPE,SIZE,URL&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.buckyverse.org&size=32&drop_404_icon=true)buckyverse.org](https://www.buckyverse.org/en/regular_polytopes/regular_polytopes.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) That exceptional symmetry is exactly the sort of thing capable of making several otherwise independent snub constraints collapse onto the same equation.

So if what you're hunting for is a **“second snub resonance” at some high dimension**, say 7D, 8D, 24D, etc., **none is presently known**. It would be a genuinely surprising new object, rather than something lurking in an established family.

And I think the really interesting next question is **whether E6,E7,E8E_6,E_7,E_8 could provide the sort of exceptional symmetry that D4/F4D_4/F_4 provides for the snub 24-cell**. That's where I'd look if we wanted to seriously hunt for a high-dimensional “snub comes back to uniform” candidate.
